unit.title: Follow principles of Occupational Health and Safety (OH&S) in work environment

summary: This unit teaches you to lead safe electrical work: to assess risks, choose controls in the right order, manage isolation for a whole team, control arc flash, work at height, in trenches and confined spaces, near batteries, generators and solar systems, and in Jamaica's heat. You will learn the duties of employers, team leaders and workers, how to run inductions, inspections and toolbox talks, what to do in an emergency, and how to investigate an incident so that it does not happen again.

blocks.p: At Level 2 you followed safety rules. At Level 3 you are responsible for the people who follow them: you plan the job, write the risk assessment and method statement, brief the team, check the controls, stop unsafe work and investigate what goes wrong. The hazards of electrical work have not changed, but your duties have.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Know the duties
Explain what the law and the employer expect of the employer, the team leader and each worker, and what to do when a worker refuses unsafe work.
Assess risk and choose controls
Identify hazards, score risk before and after controls, and choose controls down the hierarchy, with PPE last.
Lead safe isolation for a team
Plan the isolation, manage personal locks, tags, hasps and lock boxes, prove dead, deal with stored energy and run the switch-on.
Control electrical hazards
Arc flash, overhead lines, generators, solar PV, batteries, temporary supplies, wet locations and open boards.
Control other site hazards
Work at height and on fragile roofs, excavations, confined spaces, manual handling, traffic, heat, chemicals, asbestos and biological hazards.
Manage people
Site inductions, toolbox talks, consultation, lone working, fitness for work and fatigue.
Plan for emergencies
Know the isolators, first-aid kit, AED and extinguishers; rescue, first aid and burns; call for help.
Inspect and report
Carry out site safety inspections with a checklist, report all injuries, near misses and unsafe conditions, and follow actions through.
Investigate and learn
Find the root cause of an incident without blame, agree actions with owners and dates, and check that they are done.

ul: In Jamaica, workplace safety has long been covered by the **Factories Act** and its regulations, enforced by the Occupational Safety and Health Department of the **Ministry of Labour and Social Security**, which inspects workplaces and investigates serious accidents. A wider occupational safety and health law has been in preparation for some years. Your instructor will tell you which law is in force now; this kit teaches the practice that all of them expect.
Electrical work is also governed by the electrical code, based on the US National Electrical Code (NEC), and by the inspection rules of the Government Electrical Regulator.
Emergency numbers: **110** for ambulance and fire, **119** for police.
Where this kit gives a distance, a time or a temperature, it is a typical figure. Your company's procedure, JPS, the maker and your instructor have the final word.

sections.title: Duties, safety culture and leading people

head: Who
Duties
rows: **Employer**

Provide a safe workplace, safe tools and equipment, training, information, PPE, safe systems of work (such as isolation procedures), first aid and welfare; assess risks; consult workers; report and investigate incidents.
**Team leader**

Plan the work safely; write or apply the risk assessment and method statement; brief the team; check tools and PPE; supervise trainees; make sure procedures are followed; stop unsafe work; report incidents and hazards; set the example.
**Each worker**

Follow procedures and training; use PPE and equipment properly; look after their own safety and that of others; not interfere with safety equipment; report hazards, near misses and incidents; come to work fit.
Everyone on a shared site
Co-operate with the site rules and the other firms; stop unsafe acts politely, whoever is doing them, and tell the site manager.

blocks.h: When a worker refuses a task

flow: Stop that task
Thank the worker for raising it and listen, without pressure or threats
Look at the hazard together and check the risk assessment
Fix the problem, change the method, or get advice
Restart only when it is safe and the worker is satisfied
Record the concern and the action taken

blocks.p: A worker who refuses unsafe work is doing their job. A leader who punishes them teaches the whole team to stay quiet.

head: Good culture
Poor culture
rows: Anyone can stop a job they think is unsafe
Only the boss talks about safety
Near misses are reported and discussed
Near misses are hidden to keep the record clean
Procedures are followed when the job is late
Rules are skipped to catch up
Leaders wear PPE and follow isolation rules themselves
Leaders say 'do as I say, not as I do'
Workers are consulted when procedures are written
Procedures arrive from the office and nobody follows them

blocks.p: Workers are **consulted** when a safe work procedure is written because they know the real job and its hazards. A procedure written without them is often unworkable, and an unworkable procedure is ignored.

Nobody starts on a site, including an experienced electrician who joins the team today, until they have had a **site induction**: the site's hazards and rules, the emergency arrangements, the first-aiders, the assembly point, the isolators, where to report hazards, and who is in charge. Record who was inducted and when.
A toolbox talk is a short talk, about ten minutes, on one hazard the team will meet that day. Use a real example, ask questions, and record who attended.

blocks.h: Fitness for work, fatigue and lone working

ul: A worker who arrives smelling of alcohol, unsteady, or affected by drugs or medicine is **stopped from working and reported**, however embarrassing. Electrical work and ladders are not for an impaired person.

**Fatigue:** tired people make more mistakes, and in electrical work a mistake can kill. Plan shifts so that nobody works day after day of very long hours; watch for the signs; stop a worker who is too tired to be safe.

**Lone working**, for example in a remote pump house: agree **check-in calls** at set times, and what happens if a call is missed; make sure the person has a charged phone or radio with signal, knows the emergency arrangements, and does not do live work or work at height alone.

sections.title: Risk assessment, the hierarchy of controls and method statements

ul: A **hazard** is anything that could cause harm: a live busbar, a fragile roof, a battery bank.
**Risk** is the chance that the hazard causes harm, and how bad the harm would be.
A **control** is something that removes the hazard or reduces the risk.
**Residual risk** is what is left after the controls are in place.

flow: Look at the job, the site and the people
List the hazards
Decide who could be harmed, and how
Score each risk: likelihood × severity
Choose controls, down the hierarchy
Score again with the controls
Write it down, brief the team, and review it if anything changes

head: Score
Likelihood
Severity
rows: Unlikely
Minor: first aid only
Possible
Serious: time off work
Likely
Major: death or permanent injury

blocks.p: **Example.** Changing a board in a shop that stays open: 'contact with live incoming supply' is likely (3) and major (3), score 9, before controls. With the supply isolated by JPS or a competent person, locked, proved dead and the parts that must stay live shrouded, it becomes unlikely (1) and still major (3), score 3. Scoring is a way of ordering the hazards; the control is what matters.
Choose from the top down. A control higher up protects everyone all the time; PPE protects one person, only if it is worn, checked and right.

head: Level
Electrical examples
rows: 1. **Eliminate**
Plan the job so that the board is isolated and the work is done dead; arrange a full shutdown instead of live work.
2. **Substitute**
Cordless tools instead of trailing 110 V leads; a mobile tower instead of a ladder; extra-low-voltage lighting in wet places.
3. **Engineering controls**
RCD or GFCI protection, shrouds over live parts, barriers, lock-off devices, guards, dust extraction, shoring in a trench.
4. **Administrative controls**
Method statements, permits, isolation procedures, personal locks and tags, signs, briefings, training, supervision, agreed working times.
Safety boots, glasses, gloves, hard hat, hearing protection, arc-rated clothing and face shield, harness where falls cannot be prevented.

blocks.note: 'Be more careful', a warning sign and a second person watching are all weak controls: they do nothing to the hazard. Isolating the board removes it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **method statement** says how the job will be done safely, step by step: the sequence, who does what, the isolation points, the equipment, the controls from the risk assessment, and the emergency arrangements. On larger sites it is checked by the site manager before work starts. Brief the team on it at the work area, and update it when the job changes.

A **permit to work** is a written authority for a particular high-risk task: live testing, work in a confined space, hot work, work near overhead lines, work in a hazardous area. It names the people, the equipment, the controls and the time, and is signed on and signed off. It does not replace locks, tags and testing.

sections.title: Safe isolation for a team, arc flash and other electrical hazards

flow: Identify every source of supply from the drawings: JPS, generator, solar PV, UPS, control supplies
Switch off and isolate at the main isolator and at every other source
Fit a multi-lock hasp, or put the isolator key in a group lock box
Each person fits their own padlock and danger tag, with their name and the date
Prove the two-pole tester on a proving unit; prove dead at the point of work on every conductor; prove the tester again
Check for stored energy and discharge it as the maker says
Shroud and sign any parts that must stay live; barrier the area
Anyone who leaves and returns tests again before touching anything
At the end: each person confirms their work is done, tools out, covers on, and removes only their own lock
The leader checks that all locks are off and everyone is clear, announces the switch-on, switches on and records it

ul: Nobody removes another person's lock. If someone has gone home with their lock on, follow the company's procedure for removing it, which involves the supervisor confirming that the person is clear.
A **hasp** takes several padlocks on one isolator. A **group lock box** holds the key to a locked isolator; each person locks the box with their own padlock.
The person taking over a half-finished job fits their lock before the person leaving removes theirs.
A **shroud** is an insulating cover fitted over nearby live parts to stop accidental contact. Parts that must stay live, such as the incoming terminals of a main switch, are shrouded and signed.

blocks.p: Isolating the supply does not always make equipment safe. **Capacitors** in variable-speed drives, soft starters, inverters, UPS units and power-factor correction banks can stay charged for several minutes; drives often carry a label saying how long to wait. Compressed springs in breakers, raised loads, pressurised pipes and hot surfaces are stored energy too. Wait the stated time, then **test before touching**.

head: Question
Answer
rows: What is it?

A sudden release of energy when current jumps through the air between conductors, or from a conductor to earth: intense heat (an arc can reach around 20,000 °C), blinding light, a pressure blast, molten metal, and noise, all in a fraction of a second.
What causes it?

A dropped tool or loose part across live conductors; test leads or a meter on the wrong range; damaged leads; dust, damp, corrosion or vermin inside switchgear; operating faulty or badly maintained equipment; racking breakers in and out.
Why is a large switchboard worse than a house board?
The **fault current** available at a main switchboard close to the transformer is far higher, so the arc releases far more energy before the protection clears it.
What harm does it do?
Severe burns, eye damage, hearing loss, injuries from the blast and from being thrown, fire; it can kill.
How is it controlled?

**Work dead.** Where live work is unavoidable: competent people only, a permit, the right tester and leads, insulated tools, shrouds, keep others back, and **arc-rated clothing and face protection** suited to the hazard. Keep switchgear clean, dry and maintained.

blocks.note: Ordinary cotton burns; polyester and nylon melt onto the skin. Arc-rated clothing is tested to withstand a stated amount of arc energy. The level needed depends on the equipment and is set by the company's arc-flash study or procedure.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Before a scissor lift, a crane, a truck with a raised body or a long ladder goes anywhere near overhead lines, **find the safe distance** from the power company (JPS) and your company's rules, and plan the work to keep that distance. Mark the lines with goal posts or barriers, use a banksman, and if the distance cannot be kept, arrange for JPS to cover, divert or switch off the line. A common minimum for low- and medium-voltage lines is about 3 m, more for higher voltages.

head: Source
Hazard
Control
rows: Standby generator
**Backfeed**: a generator connected without a proper transfer switch can push current back into the JPS lines and kill a line worker, and can start automatically while you work
A proper changeover (transfer) switch; isolate the generator as a source; carbon monoxide: run it outdoors, away from windows
Solar PV
The panels make voltage **whenever light falls on them**, so the DC cables are live even with the inverter off; DC arcs do not go out by themselves
Treat DC cables as live; keep connectors apart until the end; cover panels where the maker allows; use DC isolators; work at the cooler times of day
Lead-acid battery bank

A short circuit across the terminals (a dropped spanner) makes a huge current and a burst of molten metal; **hydrogen** given off during charging can explode; sulphuric acid burns skin and eyes; they are heavy
Ventilated room, no flames or sparks, no smoking; insulated tools; remove rings and watches; cover terminals; eye protection, gloves and apron; eye wash and water nearby; lift with help or a trolley

blocks.p: If acid gets into the eyes or onto the skin, **rinse with plenty of clean water for at least 15 to 20 minutes** and get medical help. Do not rub the eye, and do not wait for a doctor before rinsing.

ul: A temporary site supply must be **inspected and tested** like any other, including its **earth conductor**: without an earth path, a fault leaves metal live instead of tripping the supply.

Outlets on site have RCD or GFCI protection; leads are kept off the ground where they can be damaged, and never run through standing water. A lead found in water is **isolated first**, then rerouted or replaced.
In a wet trench or tank, temporary lighting runs from a **safety extra-low voltage** supply (for example 12 V or 24 V from an isolating transformer), which cuts the shock risk in wet conditions.
An open board must never be left unattended: **close it, or barrier it and leave a person** with it. A cardboard box in front of it is not a barrier.

sections.title: Height, excavations, confined spaces, manual handling and traffic

blocks.p: Falls are among the biggest killers in construction. Apply the hierarchy: avoid work at height where you can; prevent falls with a platform, tower, lift or edge protection; and only where that is impossible, arrest the fall with a harness.

head: Equipment
Use it when
Rules
rows: Stepladder or leaning ladder
Short, light work, three points of contact possible
Inspect first; 1 in 4 angle for a leaning ladder; tie or foot it; fibreglass near electricity; never on a table, pallet or drum
**Mobile tower or lift** with guard rails
Work that lasts more than a few minutes, or needs both hands or heavy parts: fitting high-bay lights in a warehouse
Built and inspected by a trained person; wheels locked; never moved with someone on it; lift operators trained
Scaffold
Long jobs at the edge of a roof or building
Erected and inspected by competent people; guard rails and toe boards
**Fall-arrest system**: harness, lanyard and anchor
Where a fall cannot be prevented, such as on some roofs
A suitable anchor; a **rescue plan** so that a hanging person is reached within minutes; harness inspected before use

ul: **Fragile roofs**: old fibre-cement sheets, clear plastic sheets, rusted zinc and skylights break under a person. Never walk on them. Use **crawl boards** that spread the load across the purlins, with fall protection and edge protection; keep off them in rain and wind.
Falling objects: tie tools, keep parts in trays, fence the area below, wear hard hats.
Jamaican roofs: metal sheets become burning hot by mid-morning and slippery when wet; plan the work for early morning and watch the weather.

flow: Check the plans for buried services and ask the owner and the service providers
Scan the route with a cable and pipe locator and mark what is found
Dig by hand near marked services
Support the sides (shoring, trench boxes) or slope them where the trench is deep or the soil is soft
Keep spoil and plant back from the edge
Fence the trench with barriers and signs; cover or light it overnight
Provide a ladder in and out; pump out water
Check daily and after rain before anyone goes in

blocks.p: The main danger in a trench is **collapse**: a cubic metre of soil weighs well over a tonne, and a buried person cannot breathe. Soft soil, rain, vibration from traffic and spoil piled at the edge all make collapse more likely. A banksman guides the digger, and everyone near plant wears high-visibility clothing.

A cable pit, a tank, a deep manhole or a sealed plant room with poor ventilation is a **confined space**: the air can be short of oxygen, or hold toxic or flammable gas, and rescue is hard. Before anyone enters: a permit, a **trained team**, an **atmosphere test** with a gas detector, ventilation, a **standby person** who stays outside to keep watch and raise the alarm, a way to communicate, and a **rescue plan** with the equipment to carry it out. A torch and a phone are not a plan, and a standby person must never go in to attempt a rescue alone.

ul: Plan the lift: where it is going, the route, the weight. Use trolleys, drum jacks and two-person lifts for heavy items.
A cable drum is **mounted on drum jacks or a stand with a spindle** when cable is pulled off it, so that it turns freely and nobody has to hold or roll it.
Lift with the legs, back straight, load close to the body, no twisting.
Boards, transformers and battery blocks are lifted by two people or with equipment, never by one person bending over them.

blocks.p: Where the team works beside a road, a driveway or a car park used by delivery trucks: **barriers, signs and high-visibility clothing**, a planned space for the van, and a banksman for reversing vehicles. Do not park across the road to 'stop' traffic. Keep the public, especially children, out of the work area with barriers and signs, and never leave open boards, trenches or tools where they can reach them.

sections.title: Heat, chemicals, asbestos, dust, noise and health

blocks.p: Roof spaces, roofs, plant rooms and generator rooms in Jamaica can be far hotter than the air outside. The body cools itself by sweating; when it cannot keep up, heat illness follows.

head: Stage
Signs
What to do
rows: Heat cramps
Painful muscle cramps, heavy sweating
Rest in shade, drink water, stretch the muscle
**Heat exhaustion**
Heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea, pale clammy skin, fast pulse
Stop work, move to a cool place, lie down with the legs raised, loosen clothing, sip water, cool the skin with wet cloths; medical help if no better in 30 minutes
**Heat stroke**
Hot skin that may be dry, confusion, slurred speech, collapse, fits, temperature over 40 °C
**Call 110 at once.** Cool the person fast: shade, wet them down, fan them, ice packs at the neck, armpits and groin. Heat stroke kills.

ul: Plan hot work for the early morning; work in shorter spells; take breaks in the shade.
Drink water often, before you are thirsty, about a cup every 15 to 20 minutes in hot work. Sweet drinks, energy drinks and alcohol make it worse.
Light, loose, long-sleeved cotton; a hat and sunscreen outdoors. Do not remove PPE to stay cool: change the plan instead.
Let new workers get used to the heat over a week or so, and watch each other for the signs.
Read the **safety data sheet** (SDS) for any product you use: PVC solvent cement, cleaners, lubricants, battery acid, cable-pulling lubricant.
**PVC solvent cement** gives off flammable, harmful vapour: ventilate the room, keep flames and hot work away, keep the lid on, and never pour waste down a drain.
Store chemicals in their labelled containers, away from heat and food; dispose of waste as the SDS says.

blocks.p: Buildings from before the 1980s or so may contain **asbestos**: in grey fibrous sheets behind old boards and fuse gear, in fibre-cement roofing and ceilings, in pipe lagging, in some floor tiles. Its fibres, breathed in, cause lung cancer and other diseases that appear many years later. Fibres are released when the material is broken, drilled, sanded or swept.

flow: Stop work in that area at once
Move people away without disturbing the material further
Close the area off with barriers and signs
Do not sweep, vacuum or bag it
Report it to the supervisor and the client, and have it tested by a qualified person
If it is asbestos, only trained, licensed or approved specialists remove it
Record who was in the area and for how long
Restart only when the area is cleared, and check other old parts of the building before drilling

ul: Cutting chases and drilling concrete make silica dust, which scars the lungs. Use dust extraction or wet cutting, and a properly fitting respirator, not a paper dust mask.
Grinders, hammer drills and generators exceed safe noise levels: wear hearing protection and limit the time.
Long use of vibrating tools damages the nerves and blood vessels of the hands: take breaks and keep the hands warm and dry.

blocks.p: Ceiling voids, cable pits and old buildings can hold **rat droppings and urine**, bat droppings, bird nests and mould. Rat urine can carry leptospirosis, a serious disease in Jamaica. Before working there: **gloves, a mask, wet cleaning** to keep dust down (never a dry broom or compressed air), then wash your hands and face. Cover cuts. Mosquitoes breed in water left in drums and buckets on site: empty them.

ul: Cable offcuts, drums, packaging and solvent rags left in a plant room are fuel for a fire and a trip hazard. Clear them daily.
Burning PVC gives off thick black smoke with **hydrogen chloride**, an acid gas that harms the lungs and corrodes metal, and carbon monoxide. In a cable fire, get out and stay out.
Hot work (grinding, soldering with a torch) needs a fire watch and an extinguisher within reach.
Know the nearest extinguisher: CO2 or dry powder for live electrical equipment, never water.

head: Item
Check before use
rows: **Insulating gloves** (rated by class)
**In date** for their electrical test; no holes, cracks, swelling or embedded dirt; **air test**: roll the cuff to trap air and look and listen for leaks; leather protectors over them
Safety glasses and face shield
Clean, unscratched; arc-rated shield where arc flash is possible
Arc-rated clothing
Rated for the job; no melting fabrics underneath; sleeves down
Safety boots
Soles not worn through; dry
Hard hat
No cracks; not past the maker's replacement date; rated for electrical work
Harness and lanyard
Webbing and stitching sound; no burns, cuts or chemical damage; inspected by a competent person; in date
Respirator
Right filter; face fit; clean

blocks.p: PPE is the last control, not the first. It is issued free, the person is trained to use it, and it is stored dry and out of the sun, because heat and UV ruin rubber and webbing.

A **safety inspection** is a planned walk round the site with a checklist, to **find hazards early and check that the controls are working**. It is not a hunt for someone to blame. The team leader does one regularly and before a new phase of work.

head: Checklist area
Look for
rows: Electrical
Open boards, leads in water or damaged, missing RCDs, untested temporary supplies, isolators not locked
Access and height
Ladders badly set or damaged, towers without guard rails, people on fragile roofs
Excavations
Unsupported sides, spoil at the edge, no barriers, no ladder
Housekeeping and fire
Offcuts and packaging piling up, blocked escape routes, extinguishers missing
Chemicals and batteries
Unlabelled containers, no eye wash in a battery area, solvent used without ventilation
People
PPE not worn, nobody inducted, signs of heat illness or fatigue

blocks.p: Each hazard found is **rated**, photographed, and given a control, an **owner and a date** in the inspection report. The leader then checks that each action was done. A hazard found in another firm's work is stopped politely and reported to the site manager, not photographed to use against them later.

sections.title: Emergencies, first aid and returning to service

blocks.p: Before work starts, the team knows: where the **main isolators** are, so the supply can be cut fast; where the **first-aid kit, AED, fire extinguishers and eye wash** are; who the **first-aiders and fire wardens** are; the **assembly point**; the site address and directions for an ambulance; and the rescue plan for anyone at height or in a confined space. Put it in the induction, post it where it can be seen, check the equipment, and run drills.

flow: **Check for danger** and cut the supply: pull the plug, switch off, open the isolator
If you cannot cut the supply, use a dry non-conducting object to separate the person; never touch them while they may be live
Shout for help and have someone call 110 with the exact location
Check response and breathing
Not breathing normally: start CPR and send for the AED
Breathing: recovery position, treat burns, keep them warm and watched
Everyone who has had a shock sees a doctor, even if they feel fine

blocks.p: **CPR for an adult:** heel of the hand on the centre of the chest, push hard and fast, about 5 to 6 cm deep, 100 to 120 times a minute; 30 compressions to 2 breaths if trained, or compressions only. **AED:** switch it on and follow the spoken instructions. Keep going until help takes over.

ul: Cool with **running water for about 20 minutes**, once the person is safe. No ice, butter, oil or toothpaste.
Remove rings and watches before swelling starts, unless stuck.
Cover with a clean, non-fluffy dressing or cling film. Do not burst blisters.
**Electrical burns** can look small on the skin and hide deep **internal damage** along the path of the current. Every electrical burn is seen by a doctor.

head: Event
First actions
rows: Fire
Raise the alarm, get people out, cut the supply if safe, call 110, fight only a small fire with the right extinguisher and an escape route behind you
Fall from height
Do not move the person unless in danger; call 110; keep them still and warm; for a hanging harness, rescue within minutes
Trench collapse
Call 110; do not jump in; dig only from the sides with the rescue team; keep others back
Heat stroke
Call 110; cool the person fast with water, shade and fanning
Acid in the eye
Rinse with clean water for at least 15 to 20 minutes; medical help
Person down in a confined space
Do not enter; raise the alarm; use the rescue plan and equipment

flow: Repair complete and inspected
Tests passed and recorded
Everyone confirms they are clear; tools and materials out; covers on
Each person removes their own lock and tag
The leader announces the switch-on and switches on
The circuit is checked and the switch-on is recorded

blocks.p: Nobody switches a breaker on and off 'to see'. Tags are kept with the records, not thrown away. The client does not switch on 'to save time'.

sections.title: Reporting, investigating and learning from incidents

blocks.p: **All injuries, near misses and unsafe conditions** are reported: not only those that need a hospital, not only those someone saw, and not only those that damaged tools. A shock with no injury is reported, recorded and the person is checked by a doctor. Serious accidents are also reported to the authorities as the law and the company's procedure require.

flow: Make sure the injured person gets care
Make the area safe: isolate, lock off and prove dead
Keep the scene as it was where possible, and take photos
Report as the company and the law require
Talk to the injured person and witnesses soon, separately, without blame
Collect the facts: drawings, labels, the isolation record, which breaker was off, whether it was proved dead and with what
Compare what happened with the procedure
Find the root cause
Agree actions with owners and dates; check they are done; share the lessons

blocks.p: An electrician shocked on a circuit 'labelled isolated' was not just unlucky, and the weather is not the cause. The useful question is **why the labels and the isolation were wrong**: a board relabelled wrongly after an earlier change, a second supply nobody knew about, or a step of the procedure skipped because of time pressure. Fix that, and the next person is safe too. Ask 'why?' until you reach something that can be changed.

ul: Each action has an **owner and a date**, and the leader checks that it is done. Actions filed away until the next incident are worth nothing.
Typical actions: relabel the board, retrain on safe isolation, add a check of locks at every board, change the procedure, replace equipment.
Tell the team what was learned. A near miss that is shared prevents the accident; one that is hidden waits to happen again.

blocks.p: Date, time and place; the people involved and witnesses; what happened, in order, as facts; the injury and the first aid given; the controls in place (PPE worn, how the circuit was isolated); the causes; the actions, with owners and dates; signature and date. Your report-writing unit covers this in full.
Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can state the safety duties of the employer, the team leader and each worker.
I can handle a worker's refusal of unsafe work the right way.
I can describe a good safety culture, run an induction and give a toolbox talk.
I can deal with an impaired worker, fatigue and lone working.
I can carry out a risk assessment, score risk and choose controls down the hierarchy.
I can write a method statement and say when a permit to work is needed.
I can manage isolation for a team with hasps, lock boxes, personal locks, tags, shrouds and a switch-on procedure.
I can explain stored energy and why I wait and test before touching a drive's terminals.
I can explain arc flash, its causes, its harm and its controls.
I can control the hazards of overhead lines, generators, solar PV, batteries, temporary supplies and wet locations.
I can choose the right equipment for work at height and explain fragile roofs and fall arrest.
I can plan a safe excavation and say what a confined space needs before entry.
I can plan manual handling, set up a cable drum and control traffic.
I can recognise heat exhaustion and heat stroke and plan work for the heat.
I can handle chemicals, asbestos, dust, noise and rat droppings safely.
I can check insulating gloves and other PPE before use.
I can carry out a site safety inspection and write actions with owners and dates.
I can act in an electric shock emergency, give CPR and treat burns.
I can return a circuit to service safely.
I can investigate an incident to its root cause and follow the actions through.

head: Figure
What it is
rows: Ambulance and fire / police in Jamaica
15 to 20 minutes
Rinsing acid from the eyes or skin
About 20 minutes
Cooling a burn under running water
Adult CPR
About 3 m
A common minimum distance from low- and medium-voltage overhead lines; ask JPS and follow your company's rule
Several minutes
How long drive capacitors can stay charged: read the label and test
1 in 4
Leaning ladder angle
About 10 minutes
A toolbox talk

terms: Air test
Rolling an insulating glove from the cuff to trap air and show any leak.
Arc flash
A sudden release of energy when current jumps through the air between conductors.
Asbestos
A fibrous mineral in some old buildings whose dust causes lung cancer and other diseases.
Backfeed
Current flowing from a building's generator back into the power company's lines.
Fall arrest system
A harness, lanyard and anchor that stop a falling worker hitting the ground.
Fragile
Describes a roof material that would break under a person's weight.
Group lock box
A box holding an isolator's key, locked by each worker's padlock.
Hasp
A device that takes several padlocks so that several workers can lock one isolator.
Heat exhaustion
Heavy sweating, weakness and dizziness from heat; it can lead to heat stroke.
Hierarchy of controls
The order of control measures: eliminate, substitute, engineering, administrative, PPE.
Hydrogen chloride
The acidic gas given off by burning PVC.
Method statement
A written step-by-step description of how a job will be done safely.
Near miss
An event in which nobody was hurt but someone could have been.
Permit to work
A written authority for a high-risk task, stating the controls.
Risk assessment
A written check of a job's hazards, their risk and the controls.
Root cause
The underlying reason an incident happened, which, if fixed, stops it happening again.
Safety inspection
A planned walk round the site with a checklist to find hazards and check controls.
Shoring
Boards, struts or boxes that stop the sides of a trench falling in.
Shroud
An insulating cover fitted over nearby live parts.
Standby person
The person who stays outside a confined space to keep watch and raise the alarm.
Stored energy
Energy left in equipment after isolation, such as charge in capacitors.
Toolbox talk
A short safety talk to the team at the start of a job or shift.

c1.title: A board change at a Santa Cruz pharmacy
c1.text: Team leader Rohan Phillips and three electricians will replace the main distribution board of a pharmacy in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth, on a Sunday. The pharmacy has a standby generator with an automatic transfer switch and a 12 V lead-acid battery bank for its security system in a small store room. The incoming JPS supply terminals must stay live. On the morning, one electrician, Dwight, says the pharmacy's old fuse board 'looks like it has that grey fibre board behind it'.

c2.title: Warehouse lighting in Freeport, Montego Bay
c2.text: Team leader Alicia Grant's team must replace forty light fittings 6 m above the floor of a warehouse in Freeport, Montego Bay, during August. The warehouse roof has clear plastic sheets among the metal ones, and the client has offered a forklift with a pallet 'to lift the men up'. By 11 a.m. the roof space is very hot. Trainee Omar is sweating heavily, dizzy and says he feels sick.

c3.title: Shock from a 'dead' circuit in Half Way Tree
c3.text: At an office in Half Way Tree, electrician Marsha received a shock while connecting a new outlet on a circuit whose breaker was labelled 'Circuit 8: office outlets' and had been switched off. She was not badly hurt. Team leader Nicholas Burke later finds that an earlier contractor had moved circuits without relabelling the board, that no lock was fitted, and that Marsha had tested with a non-contact detector only.

c4.title: A cable trench at a Portmore school
c4.text: Team leader Kerry Walker's team must dig a 30 m trench, 1.2 m deep, for a cable to a new classroom block at a school in Portmore, St Catherine, during term time. The soil is soft and sandy and rain is forecast. A delivery driveway runs beside the route. One worker suggests saving time by piling the spoil along the trench edge and skipping the shoring 'since it is only 1.2 m'.

c5.title: A solar and battery install in Negril
c5.text: Team leader Simone Clarke's team is installing solar panels on a villa roof in Negril, Westmoreland, with a lithium battery and an inverter in the garage, which also holds the old lead-acid battery bank being charged for removal. A worker starts to unplug a panel string connector in bright sun with the inverter switched off, and another wants to drill a hole in the garage wall above the batteries.

questions.q: Which sources of supply must Rohan plan to isolate before the board is touched?
o: The JPS supply only, as the generator is off on a Sunday
The JPS supply and the generator, but not the batteries, which are only 12 V
The generator only, since the JPS terminals have to stay live
The JPS supply, the generator and the battery bank's feed
questions.why: Every source that can feed the board or the work area is identified and isolated: the JPS supply at its isolator, the generator, which the transfer switch could start when the JPS supply is lost, and the battery bank's feed. Low voltage is not the only hazard a battery brings.

questions.q: What is the best way to manage the four electricians' locks on the isolator?
o: Rohan's lock alone, as he is responsible for the job
One lock, with the key hung on the board for everyone
Tags only, since the pharmacy is closed on Sundays
A hasp or lock box, with each person's own lock and tag
questions.why: Each person is protected only by a lock that only they can remove. A multi-lock hasp or a group lock box lets all four lock the same isolation, and nobody can switch on until the last lock is off.

questions.q: The incoming JPS terminals must stay live during the job. Which control is right?
o: Paint them red so that everyone can see them
Shroud them, put up a sign and brief the team
Wrap them in PVC tape and carry on as normal
Ask the youngest worker to keep well clear of them
questions.why: Parts that cannot be isolated are covered with insulating shrouds and clearly signed, and the team is briefed on them. Tape is not rated insulation, paint protects nobody, and a warning to one person is not a control.

questions.q: What should Rohan do about Dwight's 'grey fibre board'?
o: Wet it and remove it in one piece to limit any dust
Carry on, since only drilling or sanding releases fibres
Bag it carefully and put it in the skip with the old board
Stop work there, close the area off and have it tested
questions.why: The sheet may be asbestos. Nothing is done to it: work in that area stops, people move away, the area is closed off and a qualified person tests it. Only licensed or approved specialists remove asbestos, and removing it 'carefully' still releases fibres.

questions.q: Before the new board is switched on, what must happen first?
o: Rohan removes everyone's locks so that the job can be closed
The pharmacy owner switches on, so that the firm is not liable
Everyone confirms they are clear, and each removes their own lock
The tags are torn up so that nobody is confused next week
questions.why: Each person confirms their work is done, tools are out and covers are on, then removes only their own lock. Only when all locks are off and everyone is clear does the leader announce the switch-on, switch on and record it.

questions.q: Alicia is offered the client's forklift and a pallet to lift workers to the fittings. What is the main objection?
o: A pallet has no guard rails and is not made to carry people
The forklift would block the aisles for the rest of the day
The fittings would need to be handed up to the workers one by one
Only the client's own staff may drive a forklift in the warehouse
questions.why: A pallet on forks has no guard rails, no fixed floor and no secure footing, and the load can tip. Work at height needs a proper platform such as a mobile tower or a lift with guard rails, built or run by trained people.

questions.q: Cables must be run across the roof near the clear plastic sheets. What is the right approach?
o: Walk only on the metal sheets, which look strong
Crawl on the plastic sheets to spread the weight
Run the cables at night, when the sheets are cooler
Use crawl boards and fall protection; keep off the plastic
questions.why: Clear plastic sheets are fragile and will not hold a person. Crawl boards spread the load across the purlins, and fall protection and edge protection guard against a slip or a sheet giving way. The metal sheets may be rusted and fragile too.

questions.q: What should Alicia do about Omar?
o: Give him a cold energy drink and let him carry on slowly
Send him home alone on the bus to rest
Stop him working, cool him in shade, give water and watch him
Tell him to take off his overalls and keep working in a vest
questions.why: Heavy sweating, dizziness and nausea are heat exhaustion. He stops work, rests in a cool place with his legs raised, sips water and is watched. If he is no better in about 30 minutes, or becomes confused, call 110. Energy drinks and travelling alone make it worse.

questions.q: Which plan best reduces the heat risk for the rest of the job?
o: Work straight through to finish before the hottest hours
Start early and work in short spells, with shaded breaks and water
Take off hard hats and gloves to let the body cool
Put more workers into the roof space so the job ends sooner
questions.why: Heat illness is prevented by timing and pace: start at the coolest time, rotate people, rest in shade and drink water often. Working through without breaks and removing PPE both raise the risk.

questions.q: Which question will do most to stop this happening again?
o: Was Marsha unlucky to pick that circuit?
Why were the board's labels and isolation wrong?
Was the weather hot and humid that day?
Which colour was the breaker painted?
questions.why: Investigation looks for the root cause: a board relabelled wrongly, no lock, and a non-contact detector used instead of proving dead with a two-pole tester. Fixing those protects everyone; luck and weather cannot be fixed.

questions.q: Marsha says she feels fine and wants to finish the outlet. What should Nicholas do?
o: Stop her, report the shock and send her for a medical check
Let her finish, then note the shock in the site diary
Record it only if she feels unwell later in the week
Tell her to rest for an hour and then carry on
questions.why: Every electric shock is reported and recorded, and the person is checked by a doctor, because the heart's rhythm can be upset hours later. The circuit is also properly isolated and proved dead before anyone continues.

questions.q: Which action from the investigation is written correctly?
o: Everyone to be more careful at this client's boards
Marsha to be reminded about testing when convenient
Consider whether the labels could be looked at some time
Relabel DB-1 from a circuit trace by 20 November: N. Burke
questions.why: An action names what will be done, by whom and by when, and tackles a real cause. 'Be more careful', 'when convenient' and 'consider' cannot be checked and change nothing.

questions.q: What should Nicholas do with the lesson from this incident?
o: Keep it between himself and Marsha to spare her embarrassment
Mention it to the client so that they can blame the earlier contractor
Share it with the team as a toolbox talk, without blame
File it and wait to see whether it happens again
questions.why: A minor incident is a free warning. Sharing it without blame, with the actions taken, stops the same mistake elsewhere. Hiding it teaches the team that reporting is risky.

questions.q: What should Kerry do before any digging starts?
o: Dig a quick test hole with the machine to see what is there
Check the plans, scan the route and mark any services
Ask the caretaker, who has worked there for years, and begin
Start at the end furthest from the buildings, where pipes are unlikely
questions.why: Buried power cables, water and telephone lines are found from the plans, the service providers and a locator scan before the first cut, and the team digs by hand near anything marked. Memory and guesswork are not enough.

questions.q: What is wrong with the worker's suggestion about spoil and shoring?
o: Nothing: a 1.2 m trench in sand needs no support
Shoring is only needed where the trench is deeper than 3 m
Soft sand can collapse, and spoil at the edge adds load
The spoil should go on the driveway instead, out of the way
questions.why: Soft, sandy soil can collapse at far less than 1.2 m, and rain makes it worse. Spoil piled at the edge adds weight and can fall in. The sides are shored or sloped, spoil is kept back, and the trench is checked daily and after rain.

questions.q: The trench will stay open overnight beside the driveway during term time. What is needed?
o: A rope along one side and a note to the caretaker
Nothing extra, since the school gates are locked at night
A tarpaulin laid over the trench, to hide it from the children
Barriers, signs and a cover or lighting, vehicles kept back
questions.why: An open trench next to children and delivery trucks is fenced with barriers and signs, and covered or lit overnight; vehicles are kept back from the edge. A tarpaulin hides the danger, and someone walks onto it.

questions.q: Why is the panel string connector dangerous to unplug even with the inverter off?
o: The inverter stores power for several days after switch-off
The connector is wired straight to the villa's 220 V supply
The panels make voltage in sunlight, and a DC arc persists
The lithium battery feeds the panels backwards when idle
questions.why: Solar panels generate whenever light falls on them, so the string is live regardless of the inverter. Opening a connector under DC load draws an arc that does not self-extinguish. Use the DC isolator, cover the panels where allowed, or work at dawn or dusk.

questions.q: What should Simone say about drilling above the charging lead-acid batteries?
o: Drill after wetting the wall, to keep the dust down
Do not drill there: charging gives off hydrogen, which sparks ignite
Drill quickly, since the sparks from the drill are only tiny ones
Drill, but have someone fan the air away from the batteries
questions.why: Charging lead-acid batteries give off hydrogen, which collects at ceiling level and explodes if it meets a spark. The battery area is ventilated and kept free of sparks and flames; the drilling is done elsewhere or after the batteries are removed and the room aired.

questions.q: A slipping spanner bridges the lead-acid bank's terminals and burns a worker's hand. After he is moved clear, what is the right first aid?
o: Rub the burn with ice to bring the temperature down quickly
Apply butter or oil to seal the burn from the air
Wrap it tightly in a dry towel and send him back to work
Cool it under running water for 20 minutes, then cover it
questions.why: A burn is cooled with running water for about 20 minutes, rings are removed before swelling, and it is covered with a clean, non-fluffy dressing. Ice, butter and tight towels all make it worse, and a burn like this is seen by a doctor.

questions.q: A team leader on a mixed site sees a plumber from another firm using a grinder with no guard and no eye protection. What should she do?
o: Ignore it, since he is not in her team
Photograph him to use if there is a dispute later
Report it in Friday's weekly site meeting
Stop him politely and tell the site manager
questions.why: Everyone on a shared site has a duty to stop unsafe acts, whoever is doing them. A polite word stops the danger now, and the site manager deals with the other firm. Waiting or collecting evidence leaves the hazard in place.
